title: Death of Calum mac Nèill, Niall takes the harbour-house
summary: Calum mac Nèill, harbour scribe of Seann Skell for six-and-fifty years, dies in the room above the harbour-house. The boards pass, as he had let the town see coming, to his grandson Niall mac Dhòmhnaill, the boy who once counted the hulls with a hazel stick, now a man of nine-and-twenty.

title: Dòmhnall mac Chaluim keeps the trade rolls
summary: Passed over for the boards he had expected, Calum's son Dòmhnall keeps the harbour-house's trade rolls and dues, working the office beside his own son Niall without open quarrel, though he calls the boards the queerest inheritance a man could be passed over for.

title: Niall keeps his grandfather's stick at his own elbow
summary: Niall takes down the hazel stick Calum kept since the night of the sunwise turn and sets it at his own writing-place rather than returning it to the shelf, though he puts it to no further use.

title: The lamps kept on the rite's eve
summary: On the eve nearest the day of the sunwise turn the households of Seann Skell bring small lights down to the west quay and set them along the stones the fleet sailed from, a rite grown up with no ordered beginning that Niall is the first to enter in the harbour-house's own leaves.

title: The harbour-master's count of half trade
summary: Murchadh mac Raghnaill, harbour-master of Seann Skell, sets his own reckoning of empty berths against full ones beside the boards: the harbour carries little more than half the trade it carried before the sunwise turn.

title: The rope-walks of Cuan shean let hands go
summary: With more cordage made than the lessened harbour trade can use, the rope-walks along Cuan shean's waterfront turn off hands for the first time in the memory of any walker still living there.

title: Word of a second, smaller crossing
summary: A hand off a coasting boat tells, at second or third remove, of a smaller fleet said to have sailed from the island's own shore in the years after the sunwise turn and never been heard from since. Niall hears the tale and, having no name or second mouth to stand behind it, sets it aside unwritten.

title: The first turn of the headland watch
summary: Seonag nic Dhùghaill of Ceann mhòr climbs the headland at first light and keeps it through the day, seeing nothing but open water. Other households take up a turn of their own after her, and the custom becomes Faire a' Chinn, the headland watch.

title: The west quay's old name falls from use
summary: The plain old name of the west quay falls out of common mouths at Seann Skell as carters, fish-wives and children too young to have known the fleet come to call it Cidhe an Diosail, the quay of the sunwise turn, without any single day anyone can name for the change.

title: Cidhe an Diosail entered in the harbour rolls
summary: Niall enters the west quay's new name into the harbour rolls in his own hand, letting the old name stand once beside it, struck through but not scraped. The old name, Cidhe an Iar, passes to the new fish-wharf at the strand's north end.

title: Roghnaich stands with no object
summary: In the harbour rolls the word roghnaich, to choose, begins to stand alone in a clerk's hand, meaning to have chosen the crossing, and Niall lets the usage stand in his own leaves rather than write it out in full.

title: Niall's own children who never saw the fleet
summary: Niall's eldest daughter, old enough by then to help about the harbour-house, asks whether he himself saw the ships go, having no memory of her own to set beside the wall of names she leans against.

title: Death of Alasdair Saor and his last coaster
summary: Alasdair mac Iain, Alasdair Saor, who laid the fleet's first deep keel, dies at Seann Skell at the end of summer, days after launching a sewn-plank coaster at Inis àrsaidh for a fish merchant there, his last work. Niall enters the death and the quay's new name on the same leaf.

title: Murchadh mac Raghnaill takes the berths
summary: The harbour-master of Seann Skell retires to his daughter's house up the Abhainn naomh rather than die at his post, and Murchadh mac Raghnaill, of an age with Niall mac Dhòmhnaill, takes the berths and the dues.
